segments.original: Asia has been making films since the silent era. Japan was retelling stories from kabuki theater as early as the beginning of the 20th century, while the first Indian film, Raja Harishchandra (1913), dates from 1913. Japanese cinema enjoyed its first golden age in the 1930s, with directors such as Kenji Mizoguchi (1898-1956), Yasujiro Ozu (1903-1963) and Hiroshi Shimizu (1903-1966), all making incredible films in an unmistakably Japanese style and idiom. In China, at the same time, films were being produced in the Shanghai film hub, where directors such as Yu Sun (1900-1990) opted for a realistic melodramatic style to examine the problems of the gigantic and fragile nation, beset by external threats and internal disunity.

segments.original: Until the 1950s, however, Asian cinema remained practically unknown in the West. A few Japanese films were shown in Europe and North America before World War II, as were some Indian silent films directed by the German Franz Osten (1876-1956). But it was the screening of Akira Kurosawa's (1910-1998) Rashomon (1950) at the 1951 Venice Film Festival, where it won the Golden Lion, that drew audiences around the world to the richness of Japanese cinema, starting a process that would lead to greater acclaim for Asian cinema in the West.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Kurosawa was a fitting ambassador for Japanese cinema. A liberal humanist, he dealt with seemingly universal themes, exploring the inaccessibility of truth in Rashomon and depicting a man's response to mortality in Ikiru (1952). An admirer of Western culture, he adapted the literature of his favorite authors for the screen, transplanting Dostoevsky to Hokkaido in Hakuchi (The Idiot, 1951) and blending Japanese and Jacobean theatrical traditions in his samurai Macbeth, Kumonosu Jo (Throne of Blood, 1957).

segments.original: Kurosawa's triumph in Venice helped draw the world's attention to other Japanese directors, many of whom had been making films since the silent era. The serene films from the final phase of Kenji Mizoguchi's (1898-1956) career, particularly Saikaku Ichidai Onna (The Life of Oharu, 1952), Ugetsu monogatari (Ugetsu, 1953) and Sanshô Dayû (Sansho the Bailiff, 1954), combine a profound humanism with extraordinary aesthetic beauty.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Mizoguchi's use of the moving camera is unrivaled in delicacy and precision, but his style was never merely decorative. On the contrary, it always served to visually express the emotions and circumstances of his characters. By contrast, another master of postwar Japanese cinema, Yasujiro Ozu (1903-1963), rarely moved the camera, opting for a quieter, more austere style for telling his subtle stories of the Japanese family. In films such as Banshun (Late Spring, 1949), Bakushu (Early Summer, 1951) and Tôkyô monogatari (Tokyo Story, 1953), Ozu explores the troubled relationships between parents and children with compassion and a resigned wisdom.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Akira Kurosawa is the best-known Japanese director in the world. Seven Samurai, a thrilling and humane epic, is his most enduringly popular masterpiece and also his most watched film. The electrifying, if less profound, Hollywood remake The Magnificent Seven (1960) is the most successful of the many Westerns based on Kurosawa's work - including The Outrage (1964), a reworking of Rashomon (1950), and the seminal spaghetti Western Per un pugno di dollari (A Fistful of Dollars, 1964), which Sergio Leone (1929-1989) lifted wholesale from Yojimbo (1961).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: This enjoyable cultural exchange is delightful proof of cinema's universal language and appeal. Kurosawa drew inspiration from John Ford's Westerns and made something that boldly breaks with the limited traditions of the typical Japanese jidaigeki - a period film emphasizing sword fights in a medieval Japan portrayed as a fantasy land. Seven Samurai is packed with astonishing action scenes, comic incidents, misadventures, social drama, great character development and the conflict between duty and desire, all handled with impeccable attention to realism.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The film is light, nimble and economical, doing away with unnecessary explanations. It evokes mystery and sustains a mood of apprehension - with brief shots and quick cuts making up the peasants' search for potential protectors and their pleading of their case to Kambei. There are many scenes of overwhelming visual and emotional power - a dying woman dragging herself out of a burning mill and handing her baby to Kikuchiyo, who sits in the stream in shock, sobbing and crying out: "This baby is me. The same thing happened to me", as the blazing mill wheel turns behind him. Yet the film's finest moment is its ending: the three survivors gaze at their comrades' graves while the peasants below, oblivious, turn all their attention to the joyful ritual of planting rice.

segments.original: These great directors were just the best among many notable filmmakers working in the productive postwar Japanese film industry. They include Heinosuke Gosho (1902-1981), a subtle and versatile director whose films capture an intriguing mix of moods; Kon Ichikawa (1915-2008), a virulent social critic whose best films savagely satirize postwar society; Keisuke Kinoshita (1912-1998), director of subtle, sentimental melodramas, unusual in Japan; Mikio Naruse (1905-1969), director of moving stories of strong women going through hardship; Kozaburo Yoshimura (1911-2000), director of restrained dramas, also focused on female characters; and Masaki Kobayashi (1916-1996), the humanist director of the epic war trilogy The Human Condition (1959-1961).

segments.original: This variety of content and depth went hand in hand with the films' popularity: at their peak, Japanese studios enjoyed steady commercial success and, by the end of the 1950s, were producing around 500 films a year. Only in the following decade, as Japanese audiences turned their attention to foreign films or began staying home to watch television, did the film industry enter a period of decline.

segments.original: China, as an old Confucian saying predicted, was living through interesting times. Soon after the war, directors such as Zheng Junli (1911-1969) made socially critical films and developed an innovative visual style. Junli directed Wuya yu maque (Crows and Sparrows, 1949) when Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government was about to fall and be taken over by the communists; the film was only released after the civil war.

segments.original: Many of these directors were leftists, but ironically, several of them suffered after Comrade Mao came to power. The harsh criticism of Yu Sun's Wu Xun zhuan (1950) - which tells the story of the 19th-century cultural hero Wu Xun - ushered in a period of heavy state intervention in the Chinese film industry. Nationalization and strict rules on subject matter practically stamped out cinematic creativity in the 1950s.

segments.original: The development of Korean cinema was also inhibited by politics. The Korean War ended with the peninsula divided into two separate countries, ruled by regimes of the far left and the far right, both with strict censorship. Despite this, in the 1950s South Korea produced some important films based on popular novels, such as Han Hyeong-mo's (1917-1999) Jayu buin (Madame Freedom, 1956), a story of adultery that became a major box office hit.

segments.original: At the end of that same decade, several important South Korean filmmakers emerged, among them Yu Hyun-mok (1925-2009), and in 1959 the country produced more than 100 films. segments.original: Farther west, the thriving Indian film industry began to win international admiration in the postwar period with the work of its greatest director, the Bengali Satyajit Ray (1921-1992), who drew attention with Pather Panchali (1955) and his next two films, which formed the Apu Trilogy. These films followed the life of a child from his rural origins through adolescence and adulthood, using personal experience as a microcosm of life in India.

segments.original: Ray went on making incredible films in the following decades, such as Charulata (The Lonely Wife, 1964), a profound study of a married woman's loneliness. Later, he made his masterpiece, Meghe Dhaka Tara (The Cloud-Capped Star, 1960), about the tragic experience of a refugee woman in Calcutta.

segments.original: In Sri Lanka, Lester James Peries (b. 1919), generally considered the country's finest filmmaker, debuted in 1956 with Rekava. Sinhalese cinema, like Bollywood, was dominated by stylized melodrama, but Peries's film brought a new realism to it with the story of the punishments inflicted on a boy who believes he has magical powers. Peries expresses a subtle critique of the country's traditional beliefs. There are also active film industries in the Philippines, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Pakistan, Iran and Central Asia.
